questions.q: You have just made a bug happen on purpose with a one-line command. According to the method, what comes next?
questions.explain: Observe, reproduce, isolate, hypothesize, test, fix, verify. After reproducing comes isolating: a minimal reproduction removes most of the program from suspicion before you start guessing causes.
options: Fix: you know where the bug is now
Isolate: shrink the input and the code until everything left is needed
Verify: check that the command still fails
Observe: read the bug report again

questions.q: A developer cannot reproduce a crash, changes a line that "looks risky", deploys, and the crash has not happened for a day. What is wrong with calling it fixed?
questions.explain: If you cannot make the bug happen on demand, you cannot tell whether a change fixed it. "It hasn't happened again" is also what you would see if the fix did nothing. Reproduce first, then the same reproduction proves the fix.
options: Nothing: a day without the crash proves the fix
They should have waited a week instead of a day
Without a reproduction there is no evidence: the crash may simply not have been triggered yet
Risky-looking lines are never the cause

questions.q: You change the price parser, the rounding function and the cache timeout at once, and the wrong totals disappear. What do you now know?
questions.explain: Changing one thing at a time is what makes an experiment tell you something. With three changes, the result cannot separate their effects, and the unneeded changes may introduce new bugs.
options: All three changes were needed
The price parser was the cause, because it was changed first
That one or more of the changes helped, but not which one, and not whether the others broke something
That the bug was in the cache

questions.q: A report says: "The payment page is broken, Tunde paid ₦5,000 for a ₦50,000 order at 14:10." Which part is an interpretation rather than a fact?
questions.explain: The amounts and the time can be checked in the database. "The payment page is broken" names a suspect. The wrong amount could come from the cart, the catalogue, a discount or a conversion; don't let the report choose where you look.
options: Tunde paid ₦5,000
The order was worth ₦50,000
It happened at 14:10
The payment page is broken

questions.q: Wrong totals started "since yesterday afternoon". What is the most useful next observation?
questions.explain: Bugs rarely appear out of nowhere. Something changed just before the first bad result. In the lesson it was a price import at 15:39, three minutes before the first wrong order.
options: Read the checkout code from the top
Find out what changed around then: deployments, imports, configuration, dependency updates
Restart the server
Ask the customer which browser they use

questions.q: Where should you start reading this trace?
questions.explain: The library threw because it received undefined instead of an email. Your first frame shows what you passed in. Skip node:internal frames, and treat library frames as "where it failed", not "who is wrong".
questions.code:
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'toLowerCase')
    at normalizeEmail (file:///app/node_modules/mail-tools/index.js:12:18)
    at findUser (file:///app/src/users.js:31:22)
    at login (file:///app/src/auth.js:8:26)
    at node:internal/process/task_queues:105:5
options: At node:internal/process/task_queues, because it is the bottom of the stack
At mail-tools/index.js, because the library has a bug
At findUser in src/users.js:31: the first frame in your own code, where you passed something to the library
At login, because it is the entry point

questions.q: What does the word async in at async startShop (file:///home/you/shop/load.js:9:20) tell you?
questions.explain: V8 records async stack traces: frames of functions that were suspended at an await. Without them you would not see who awaited the function that failed.
options: That startShop threw the error itself
That startShop was waiting at an await on line 9 when the error happened further down
That the frame belongs to Node.js, not your code
That the error happened in a different thread

questions.q: An error thrown inside a setTimeout callback shows sendReminder and Timeout._onTimeout, but not scheduleReminders, which set the timer. Why?
questions.explain: A stack trace is the call stack at the moment of the error. By the time the timer fired, the function that scheduled it was long finished. Only await keeps async frames; timers, events and callback APIs do not.
options: The stack trace limit cut it off
Timers run on a separate thread
The callback ran later on a fresh call stack; scheduleReminders had already returned
Arrow functions do not appear in stack traces

questions.q: Node.js prints Error: Could not load order 1042 and, indented below it, [cause]: Error: ENOENT: no such file or directory, open './orders/1042.json'. How do you read the two parts?
questions.explain: Wrapping with new Error(message, { cause }) keeps both levels: the meaning (loading order 1042 failed) and the detail (the file is missing, and the relative path shows where the program looked).
options: Two unrelated errors happened at the same time
The outer error says what failed; the cause says why, at the lower level
The cause is a warning and can be ignored
The outer error is from Node.js, the cause from your code

questions.q: Why does throw "Insufficient funds" make debugging harder than throw new Error("Insufficient funds")?
questions.explain: An Error captures the call stack when it is constructed. A thrown string carries only its text. In an ES module, the uncaught output does not even name the file or the line.
options: Strings cannot be caught with catch
A string has no stack: the stack is recorded when an Error object is created, so nothing says where it was thrown
Strings are converted to numbers when thrown
Node.js refuses to print thrown strings

questions.q: A crash deep inside a long middleware chain shows ten frames, all inside the middleware library, and none of your route code. What is the quickest way to see more?
questions.explain: V8 records 10 frames by default. When the interesting frames are further down, raise the limit for the debugging session.
options: Wrap every function in try/catch
Run once with node --stack-trace-limit=50 (or set Error.stackTraceLimit) so more frames are recorded
Switch the project to CommonJS
Stack traces can never show more than ten frames

questions.q: Production charged ₦666 for order 1042. Your reproduction script prints ₦0. What should you conclude?
questions.explain: A reproduction should fail the same way production does. A different wrong answer can come from a mistake in the repro itself (wrong data, missing setup) and send you after the wrong cause.
options: The bug is reproduced, since both numbers are wrong
You may be looking at a different bug: bring the repro closer to production until it gives the same wrong ₦666
Production must be using a different currency
Fix the ₦0 first, then ₦666 will go away

questions.q: Your local run of the import gives correct prices, but the server's import does not. Which is the right next step?
questions.explain: When a bug does not reproduce, the difference between the two environments is the bug. Narrow it down one difference at a time, starting with the exact input data.
options: Declare it a server problem and restart it
Add random delays until it fails locally
List what differs (the exact input file, Node.js version, time zone, locale, environment variables, state) and bring the local run closer one item at a time
Ask users to stop importing

questions.q: Which is not a benefit of a minimal reproduction?
questions.explain: A minimal repro makes the bug small enough to explain; it does not fix anything. It still fails, and that failure becomes your regression test.
options: It removes most of the program from suspicion
It is easy to hand to a colleague or an issue tracker
Making it often reveals the bug on its own
It fixes the bug, because small code cannot fail

questions.q: Which is the most useful hypothesis?
questions.explain: A useful hypothesis names one mechanism and makes predictions that could turn out false. This one predicts a sharp boundary at ₦1,000 that you can test in one line.
options: "The import code is buggy."
"Something is wrong with numbers."
"parseFloat stops at the thousands comma, so every price of ₦1,000 or more is wrong and every price below is right."
"It might be the cache, or the discounts, or the parser."

questions.q: Two hypotheses explain "only expensive items are charged wrongly": (A) a discount rule misfires on expensive items, (B) the imported prices are wrong. Which single observation separates them?
questions.explain: A predicts correct catalogue prices and a wrong total; B predicts wrong catalogue prices. Printing the imported prices kills one of them immediately. Good tests are chosen because the hypotheses disagree about their result.
options: Whether the bug happens on weekends
Whether the prices stored in the catalogue are correct
Whether customers complained
Whether the total is shown in naira

questions.q: While debugging, why is console.log(order) usually better than console.log(JSON.stringify(order)) in Node.js?
questions.explain: console.log uses util.inspect, which shows values as they are: strings in quotes, undefined fields, Map entries. JSON is a data format, not a debugging view.
options: JSON.stringify is slower
JSON.stringify drops undefined fields and turns a Map into {}, hiding facts you may need
console.log sorts the keys
JSON.stringify cannot print strings

questions.q: In Chrome, you log a cart, then the code adds an item, then you expand the logged cart in the console. What do you see?
questions.explain: Browser consoles show logged objects live: expanding reads the current values. Log a copy (structuredClone(cart)) or specific fields when the object changes later.
options: The cart as it was when it was logged
The cart as it is when you expanded it, including the item added later
An error, because the object changed
Only the first level of the cart

questions.q: A loop processes 50,000 orders, and stock goes negative somewhere. Why is console.assert(stock >= 0, ...) a good tool here?
questions.explain: console.assert stays silent until its condition is false, so you get one line at the exact moment it matters, instead of 50,000 lines to scroll through. (It does not throw.)
options: It stops the program at the first failure
It prints nothing while the condition holds, and prints the message only on the iteration where it fails
It fixes negative stock automatically
It throws an error that crashes the loop

questions.q: Which change fixes the root cause of the ₦8,500 → ₦8 import bug?
questions.explain: The database fix disappears at the next import. Removing one comma breaks on ₦1,250,000.00. The root cause is a parser that silently accepts text it does not understand; the fix understands every valid format and fails loudly on the rest.
options: Correct the rice price in the database
Replace the first comma with replace(",", "")
Parse the whole price format (all commas, naira and kobo as whole numbers) and refuse any text that does not match it
Round totals to the nearest ₦1,000

questions.q: Why should you run a new regression test against the old, buggy code once?
questions.explain: The proof that a test guards against the bug is that it fails when the bug is present. If it passes on both versions, it tests something else.
options: To measure how slow the old code was
A test that also passes on the buggy code does not test the bug at all
Test runners require it
To update the snapshot

questions.q: You have been stuck for 45 minutes. What makes the best question to a colleague, an issue tracker or an AI assistant?
questions.explain: Whoever answers needs the same facts you needed. A minimal repro plus your ruled-out hypotheses lets them skip what you already did. And whatever answer comes back is still a hypothesis: test it against your repro.
options: The whole repository and "it doesn't work"
The error message only
A minimal reproduction, what you expected, what happened, and the hypotheses you already ruled out
A screenshot of the running app

questions.q: Every order is being undercharged right now. What comes first?
questions.explain: Stop the bleeding first. A mitigation is not a fix, but it buys time to debug properly. Experimenting on live production code adds a second problem to the first.
options: A careful root-cause analysis
A mitigation that stops the loss (pause checkout or roll back the price list), then the method
Editing the live server code to experiment
Writing the regression test

questions.q: Which log line would have revealed the price bug straight from yesterday's import log?
questions.explain: A structured line with the raw input and the parsed result side by side makes the mismatch visible without any reproduction. A fixed event name and the ids make such lines easy to search.
options: console.log("importing...")
console.log(800)
{"event":"catalogue.import.row","sku":"RICE-5","raw":"₦8,500.00","priceKobo":800}
console.log("done")

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: parseFloat reads as far as it can and stops at the comma, giving 8. Number requires the whole string to be a number, so it gives NaN. Neither understands thousands separators.
options: 8 NaN 650
NaN NaN 650

questions.q: This is the shop's original parser. What does it print?
questions.explain: ₦999.99 has no comma and is right. ₦1,000.00 is read as 1, so 100 kobo, and ₦2,400.50 as 2, so 200 kobo. This is the sharp boundary the hypothesis predicted.
options: 99999 NaN NaN

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 0 + 1000 is 1000. 1000 + "2000" is string concatenation: "10002000". From then on every += appends: "100020003000". One text value poisons the rest of the total.
options: 6000 number
03000 string
NaN number

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON has no undefined, so the field is left out, and a Map has no own enumerable properties, so it becomes {}. Two facts vanished from your debugging output.
questions.code:
const line = { sku: "EGG-30", discount: undefined, tags: new Map([["fresh", true]]) };
console.log(JSON.stringify(line));
options: {"sku":"EGG-30","discount":undefined,"tags":{"fresh":true}}
{"sku":"EGG-30","discount":null,"tags":{}}
{"sku":"EGG-30","tags":{"fresh":true}}

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Shorthand properties turn each variable name into a key, so the log is labelled for free. console.log prints objects with util.inspect style: unquoted keys, strings in single quotes.
options: { sku: 'RICE-5', quantity: 2, lineTotal: 1600 }
{ "sku": "RICE-5", "quantity": 2, "lineTotal": 1600 }
[object Object]

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each label keeps its own counter for the whole program. The last call is the third time "paid" is counted.
options:
paid: 1
unpaid: 1
paid: 2
paid: 3

paid: 1
unpaid: 1
paid: 2
paid: 1

paid: 2
unpaid: 1

paid
unpaid
paid
paid

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: console.assert prints only when its condition is false, here on the third iteration, and it does not throw, so the loop finishes and done -1 is printed.
options:
Assertion failed: stock went negative: -1
done -1
done -1
Assertion failed: stock went negative: -1

stock went negative: 2
stock went negative: 1
Assertion failed: stock went negative: -1
done -1

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The outer error keeps the inner one in cause. The inner error was created without a cause, so its cause is undefined. The chain ends there.
options:
could not reserve RICE-5
no stock row for RICE-5
undefined

no stock row for RICE-5
could not reserve RICE-5
undefined

could not reserve RICE-5
undefined
undefined

could not reserve RICE-5: no stock row for RICE-5
undefined
undefined

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: What was thrown is exactly what is caught: a string. Strings have no stack property, and a string is not an Error. There is nothing to tell you where it came from.
options: string undefined false
object undefined true
string Insufficient funds false
Error Insufficient funds true

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: order.items is undefined (the data says lineItems), and reading .map from undefined throws. The message names the property being read, map, so the question to ask is why the thing before it is undefined.
options: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')
TypeError: order.items.map is not a function
ReferenceError: items is not defined
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'items')

questions.q: This shrinker removes one item at a time while the test still fails. What does it print?
questions.explain: A and D can be removed and the cart still fails. Removing B (the only negative quantity) or C (the only coupon) makes it pass, so both stay. The minimal cart shows that the bug needs both conditions, which is itself a clue.
options: B,C
B
C
A,B,C,D

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: cause stores the very same object you passed, so the identity check is true. The outer error keeps its own name; the cause keeps its own.
options: true RangeError Error
false RangeError Error
true Error RangeError
true RangeError RangeError

questions.q: Write parsePrice(text) that turns prices like "₦8,500.00", "₦650" or "1,250,000.50" into whole kobo, using no floating-point arithmetic. It must throw an Error for any text that is not in this format.
questions.explain: Validate the whole shape first, so nothing is guessed. Then split naira and kobo and convert each with Number: whole numbers stay exact, where parseFloat(...) * 100 could drift.

questions.q: The "compare" part of testing a hypothesis: write firstDifference(expected, actual) that returns the index of the first position where the two arrays disagree, or -1 if they are the same (including the same length).
questions.explain: Loop to the longer length, so an extra or missing element counts as a difference (undefined !== 290). The first disagreement is where to look: the bug is at or just before that step.

questions.q: Finish shrink(items, stillFails): repeatedly try removing one item; if the smaller list still fails, keep it and start again; stop when no single item can be removed. Then shrink the order list to the minimal failing one.
questions.explain: Orders 1, 3 and 5 can go and the list still fails. Removing 2 (the only paid order before the refund) or 4 (the only refund) makes it pass. The result, a paid order followed by a refund, is the smallest case to explain.

questions.q: Write a tiny reproduction helper check(label, actual, expected) that prints PASS label when the values are strictly equal and FAIL label: got X, expected Y otherwise. Use it to show the bug in the old parser.
questions.explain: A repro that checks itself does not rely on you remembering the right answer. Printing both the actual and the expected value turns every failure into an observation.

questions.q: Write describeChain(error) that returns the messages of an error and all its causes, joined with " <- " (outermost first).
questions.explain: Follow cause until it is undefined. The outer message says what failed, each cause says why one level lower. Logging the whole chain keeps both.
questions.expected:
GET /orders/1042 failed <- could not load order 1042 <- ENOENT: orders/1042.json
ENOENT: orders/1042.json

questions.q: Test the hypothesis "every price with a thousands comma is parsed wrongly and every other price is right". For each price, print the text and ok or WRONG by comparing the old parser with the correct kobo value. The prediction holds if exactly the comma prices are wrong.
questions.explain: The boundary pair ₦999.99 / ₦1,000.00 is the sharpest test: the hypothesis predicts one right and one wrong. Had ₦350.00 come out wrong, the hypothesis would be dead.

questions.q: Fix the bug at the boundary: write toSubtotal(input) that converts form input to a whole number of kobo and throws for anything that is not a non-negative integer. Then the cart total must be 6000.
questions.explain: Converting once, where data enters the program, means the rest of the code only ever sees numbers. Validating at the same place turns a silent wrong total into a loud, specific error.
